core: Constructivism as an account of knowledge-building: learners assemble understanding out of prior structures rather than receiving it intact
Cognitive constructivism (Piaget): schemes, assimilation, accommodation, disequilibrium, and equilibration
Social constructivism (Vygotsky): social origin of higher mental functions, mediation by signs and psychological tools, and the zone of proximal development
Scaffolding: introduced as an instructional concept by Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976), not by Vygotsky; contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility as its defining features
The central distinction of the topic: constructivism as a theory of learning versus constructivist instruction as a family of teaching methods, and the inference that links them

The minimal-guidance debate: Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006) against minimally guided instruction; the replies from Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, and Chinn (2007) and Schmidt, Loyens, van Gog, and Paas (2007); the Sweller, Kirschner, and Clark (2007) reply
What U.S. evidence reviews actually rate: the 2021 IES/WWC elementary mathematics intervention practice guide and the 2012 WWC single study review of a problem-based economics curriculum
Why 'each learner constructs knowledge' does not license 'all constructions are equally valid'
supporting: Prior knowledge and preconceptions as the first key finding of the National Research Council's How People Learn synthesis
Worked-example effect and expertise reversal as the cognitive-load case for guidance
Meta-analytic pattern for problem-based learning reported by Hmelo-Silver et al.: no effect on declarative knowledge tests, moderate effect favoring PBL on knowledge application
'More knowledgeable other' as a later summarizing label for the helper role named in the translated definition of the zone of proximal development
Piaget's four developmental periods, mentioned only to place the mechanism in context
outOfScope: Behaviorism, cognitivism, and social learning theory beyond one sentence of contrast (separate topics in this unit)
Piaget's stages in detail and their empirical status (education:educational-psychology:cognitive-development)
Cognitive load theory as a full topic in its own right
Constructivism in sociology, philosophy of science, or international relations
Learning-styles claims, which the subject source-map flags as unsupported
Individualized instructional or clinical advice about a particular student or program

claims.claim: Constructivism's descriptive core - that learners build new understanding out of what they already know - is accepted on both sides of the instructional debate; Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, and Chinn open their defense of problem-based and inquiry learning by stating that all learning involves knowledge construction and is therefore a constructivist process, and locate the real dispute in which instructional practices promote that construction.

The National Research Council's How People Learn synthesis states as its first key finding that students come to the classroom with preconceptions about how the world works, and that if their initial understanding is not engaged they may fail to grasp new concepts, or learn them for a test and revert to their preconceptions afterward.

In Piaget's account, adaptation is a process of equilibration between assimilation and accommodation: assimilation integrates an aspect of the environment into an existing scheme, while accommodation modifies the scheme itself to encompass something it could not yet absorb.
The instability produced when an existing scheme cannot absorb a new case is what triggers accommodation, and repeated cycles of disequilibrium and accommodation settle into a new equilibration.

Piaget classified development into four sequential periods: sensorimotor (birth through roughly 18 to 24 months), preoperational (about ages 2 to 7), concrete operational (about ages 7 to 11), and formal operational (from about age 11).

In Vygotsky's account, higher mental functions have a social origin: the tools of social behavior are transformed into instruments of individual psychological organization, and cultural signs and instruments - language above all - mediate mental development.

The zone of proximal development is defined in the standard English translation of Vygotsky as the distance between the actual developmental level determined by independent problem solving and the level of potential development determined through problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers.

The term 'scaffolding' entered education as an instructional concept through Wood, Bruner, and Ross, 'The Role of Tutoring in Problem Solving' (Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 1976, 17(2), 89-100), where it names adult support that lets a child achieve what would be beyond unassisted effort; its association with Vygotsky's zone of proximal development was made by the later literature rather than by Vygotsky.

The flat statement that 'Vygotsky never used the scaffolding metaphor' overstates the history: Shvarts and Bakker trace uses of the metaphor to Nikolai Bernstein and Alexander Luria and to Vygotsky's notebooks, while still identifying Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976) as the point at which the concept was empirically introduced.

A decade-spanning review of scaffolding research identifies contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility as the three key characteristics of scaffolding, reports that the number of effectiveness studies available was small although results suggested scaffolding is effective, and identifies measurement as the main challenge in the field.

Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark argue that instructional programs using minimal guidance treat the pedagogic content of a learning experience as identical to the methods and processes - that is, the epistemology - of the discipline being studied, and that this may be a fundamental error.

Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006) argue from human cognitive architecture and expert-novice differences that minimally guided instruction is less effective and less efficient than instruction that strongly guides the learning process, cite the worked-example effect as among the strongest evidence for guidance, and state that the advantage of guidance begins to recede only when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance.

Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, and Chinn (2007) reply that Kirschner and colleagues mistakenly conflated problem-based learning and inquiry learning with discovery learning, that both approaches employ scaffolding extensively and thereby reduce cognitive load, and they report that a meta-analysis by Dochy and colleagues found no effect of PBL on declarative knowledge tests but a moderate effect size favoring PBL students on measures of knowledge application.

Schmidt, Loyens, van Gog, and Paas (2007) agree that minimally guided approaches are less effective for novices, but reject the equation of problem-based learning with minimal guidance, arguing that PBL flexibly adapts guidance and is compatible with human cognitive architecture; Sweller, Kirschner, and Clark (2007) reply by reasserting the need for randomized controlled comparisons that alter one variable at a time and by rejecting the view that presenting relevant information should be reduced in favor of teaching learners how to find information.

Mayer (2004), reviewing research on discovery of problem-solving rules, conservation strategies, and LOGO programming strategies, concluded that guided discovery was more effective than pure discovery for learning and transfer in each case, and that the constructivist view of learning may be best supported by instruction involving cognitive rather than behavioral activity, instructional guidance rather than pure discovery, and curricular focus rather than unstructured exploration.

The March 2021 IES/What Works Clearinghouse practice guide 'Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades' issues six recommendations, the first of which is to provide systematic instruction during intervention to develop student understanding of mathematical ideas, and assigns it a strong level of evidence.

The June 2012 What Works Clearinghouse single study review of a randomized trial of the Problem Based Economics curriculum found the study met WWC evidence standards with reservations because of high teacher attrition, and reported no statistically significant difference in students' economics knowledge while noting an effect size of 0.29 that was positive and large enough to be considered substantively important under the WWC's threshold of at least 0.25 standard deviations.

Constructivism as an account of process does not entail that all constructions are equally warranted: the How People Learn synthesis treats unengaged preconceptions as misconceptions that persist, and Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark note evidence that unguided instruction may have negative results when students acquire misconceptions or incomplete or disorganized knowledge.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether constructivist, discovery, problem-based, and inquiry teaching should be treated as one pedagogically equivalent family that the evidence disfavors
positions: Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006): these differently named approaches are essentially pedagogically equivalent, and half a century of controlled research favors strong instructional guidance, especially for novices; the worked-example effect and the expertise reversal effect explain why.

Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, and Chinn (2007): problem-based and inquiry learning are highly scaffolded rather than minimally guided, so lumping them with unguided discovery misdescribes them; the evidence base they cite includes a meta-analysis showing a moderate advantage for PBL on knowledge application with no effect on declarative knowledge.
Schmidt, Loyens, van Gog, and Paas (2007): agree that novices need guidance, but argue PBL adapts guidance flexibly and is compatible with human cognitive architecture.

Sweller, Kirschner, and Clark (2007): reassert randomized controlled comparisons altering one variable at a time and reject reducing the presentation of relevant information in favor of teaching learners to find information.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Reported as an open, named exchange with no winner declared. The lesson states the point all four papers agree on - that learners construct knowledge and that novices need guidance - and locates the live disagreement in what counts as guidance, whether the named approaches actually deliver it, and which outcomes should be measured.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Vygotsky used the scaffolding metaphor
positions: The common teacher-preparation claim that scaffolding is Vygotsky's own concept.
The common correction that Vygotsky never used the term and that it belongs to Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976).
Shvarts and Bakker (2019): the concept was empirically introduced by Wood, Bruner, and Ross in 1976, but the metaphor itself appears earlier in Bernstein and Luria and in Vygotsky's notebooks.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson credits the instructional concept to Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976), states that the link to the zone of proximal development was drawn by later researchers, and adds the historical qualification rather than repeating the flat 'Vygotsky never used the word' claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What federal evidence reviews imply about constructivist instruction
positions: The 2021 WWC elementary mathematics intervention guide rates systematic instruction as supported by strong evidence for students who are struggling.

The 2012 WWC single study review of a problem-based economics curriculum found a non-significant but substantively important effect size of 0.29 in a randomized trial that met standards with reservations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported without treating either as a verdict on constructivism. The lesson states explicitly that practice guides rate practices, not philosophies, and that neither review adjudicates a theory of knowledge.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing of constructivism as 'a foundational concept in Education' that students use 'to organize information' - no source treats constructivism this way, and the draft contained no theory content whatsoever.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills words rather than constructivist terminology.
The draft's quick-check items tested only the generic habit of defining a term and applying it, not any constructivist claim.
The draft's analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no explanatory content and is on the acceptance gate's boilerplate blocklist.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with the actual theory: Piagetian assimilation, accommodation, disequilibrium, and equilibration; Vygotskian mediation, social origin of higher mental functions, and the zone of proximal development.
Made the epistemology-versus-pedagogy distinction the spine of the lesson, since that is where the discipline's actual argument sits.
Corrected the widespread misattribution of 'scaffolding' to Vygotsky, and then qualified the correction itself using the 2019 historical study rather than repeating the equally sloppy counter-claim.
Represented the minimal-guidance debate with all four papers in the 2006-2007 exchange and declined to declare a winner.
Added what U.S. evidence reviews actually rate, with the WWC ratings and the 0.29 effect size reported precisely, including the significance and attrition caveats.
Added the relativism misreading to Common Mistakes, with the correction grounded in sources from both sides of the pedagogical debate.

sourceRecords.title: Should There Be a Three-Strikes Rule against Pure Discovery Learning?
sourceRecords.provider: Mayer, R. E.; American Psychologist 59(1), 14-19 (2004); ERIC EJ684214

sourceRecords.title: How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School - Expanded Edition

Used for the first key finding - that students arrive with preconceptions about how the world works and that unengaged initial understandings leave them unable to grasp new concepts or liable to revert after a test - and for the accompanying implication that teachers must draw out and work with existing understandings. sourceRecords.title: WWC Review of the Report 'Effects of Problem Based Economics on High School Economics Instruction' (June 2012)
sourceRecords.provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education; ERIC ED533124
sourceRecords.notes: Full PDF retrieved from the ERIC full-text service and read directly. Reviews the randomized trial reported in NCEE 2010-4002 (128 teachers from 106 schools in Arizona and California; analytic sample of 64 teachers after high teacher attrition). Used for: the rating that the study meets WWC evidence standards with reservations; the finding of no statistically significant difference in grade 11-12 students' economics knowledge; and the effect size of 0.29, which the WWC describes as positive and large enough to be considered substantively important under its threshold of at least 0.25 standard deviations.
